after.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-x$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}2xy\,dx+x\,dy=$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-x.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+(2t-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2t({t}^{2}-t)\cdot 1+t(2t-1)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{t}^{3}-t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}]-[0] \\  & =8-2 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+(t+1)^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2(t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$

content.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(0,-1)$ to point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy=$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1+{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1+1)\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{4}-5{t}^{2}+2{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}(2)^{3}+\frac{{2}^{6}}{3}]-[0] \\  & =32-\frac{40}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2ydx+xdy, where C is part of the circle x2+y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(−2,0).

a
4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt
b
 4∫0πsin2⁡t(1−4cos2⁡t)dt
c
 2∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2sin2⁡t)dt
d
 8∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2cos2⁡t)dt
e
 8∫0πcos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize C by x=2cos(t), y=2sin(t), 0≤t≤π. Then dx=-2sin(t)dt and dy=2cos(t)dt, so x²y dx+x dy=4cos²(t)(1-4sin²(t))dt, giving option a directly. Option b has the same integral value by the substitution t↦π-t and symmetry interchanging sin² and cos² over [0,π]; this does not affect the validity of a.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$
after.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2ydx+xdy=∫0πx2ydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫0π(x2ydxdt+xdydt)dt=∫0π(2cos⁡t)2⋅(2sin⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅2cos⁡tdt=∫0π−16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt=4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt

content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$
content.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Write the integrand as x dx+y dy+x dy-y dx. The first two terms integrate to [(x²+y²)/2] from (0,3) to (-2,0), giving -5/2. Parametrize the counterclockwise arc by x=2cos(t), y=3sin(t), π/2≤t≤π. Then x dy-y dx=6dt, whose integral is 3π. The total is 3π-5/2=(6π-5)/2.

after.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-2,0).$
after.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(x-y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x+y)\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }((x-y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+6t]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[(-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )+6\pi )-(-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+3\pi )] \\  & =(-\frac{5}{4}+6\pi )-(\frac{5}{4}+3\pi ) \\  & =3\pi -\frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pi -5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-2,0).$
content.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(x-y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x+y)\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }((x-y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+6t]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[(-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )+6\pi )-(-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+3\pi )] \\  & =(-\frac{5}{4}+6\pi )-(\frac{5}{4}+3\pi ) \\  & =3\pi -\frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\pi -5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
